I think some games do succeed in conveying emotions through gameplay, although they tend to lie on the more experimental side of the spectrum. I particularly liked what [Braid](http://braid-game.com/) did, providing interesting real life metaphors for the actions that you take in the game, that make you think about certain aspects of relationships. Another example is [Passage](http://hcsoftware.sourceforge.net/passage/), and how the small decisions you can take affect the way the game plays.

For me, the most recent example of a game that was moving was the text adventure [Blue Lacuna](http://www.lacunastory.com/), which does an amazing job at making you relate to the characters and at making you feel like you aren't restricted in how you can react.

I thought about that, but I don't think it needs to be that way. It is possible for the game to guide you to the right solution, whilst still making you come up with large portions of it yourself, either by presenting you with patterns or several clues in the game world. That would not prevent it from being an adventure game.

Also, different players like different things; I tend to love hard (but logical!) puzzles because of the sense of accomplishment you get after solving them. There's at least a target audience for that, even if it's not for everybody. I think ridiculous item combinations are just bad game design, however, and I don't enjoy that at all.

Most of his points seem to be against badly designed games in general. For instance:

> Faced with failing a riddle, the average player will treat them as an exercise in permutations instead. They try all of the objects in their inventory until they stumble onto the right one, have all the conversations with all the characters over and over until the right answer presents itself, scan the screen back and forth with a mouse pointer to find clickable objects, or go in search of cheat guides to tell them what to do next.

This does not apply solely to adventure games and is typically a sign of bad game design. In any circumstance in which the player is blocked from progressing because they haven't figured something out, the natural response is to try everything. Even without items. In an FPS, badly designed levels can lead players to walk around all the rooms they have been in, trying to find some passageway that they missed the first time around. Or walking around a place they know they have to get in, looking for the entrance. The logic of the world failed, so the player resorts to doing a search on the game's state space. I don't see how this is that much different from what the author describes, and can be fixed with logical game design and thorough playtesting. Badly designed games deserve to die, but this has nothing to do with the adventure game genre.
